topics.title: Drug Metabolism: Phase I & Phase II
topics.productionRationale: Phase I (CYP450 oxidation/reduction/hydrolysis) vs phase II (conjugation) metabolism with the key inducers and inhibitors — shared page 252 with elimination-of-drugs, distinct subsections (the p196 shared-page convention).

textbookVisuals.sourceBook: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 2026
textbookVisuals.visualPurpose: The phase I/II metabolism flow figure (book 230, top half)
textbookVisuals.sourceFigureDescription: VECTOR FLOW FIGURE (pdfimages: zero raster images; VLM confirmed on ph3-vlm-census.ts): Lipophilic drugs → Phase I (predominantly CYP450-dependent) with the three reaction chutes Reduction / Oxidation / Hydrolysis → Slightly polar metabolite (active or inactive) + Reactive oxygen metabolites (label printed twice — at the phase I output and beside the phase II header) → Phase II with the four conjugation chutes Methylation / Acetylation / Glucuronidation / Sulfation → Very polar, hydrophilic metabolite (except acetylated metabolite) → Excretion: Serum (urine, sweat), bile (stool); the figure's second input, Polar drugs (water-soluble), bypasses phase I and feeds phase II directly. No margin notes or mnemonics.
textbookVisuals.kypLocation: the registry visual (MetabolismPhaseMap in visuals/pharm-p3.tsx — the pipeline zone with the input chips, bypass lane, CYP450 reactor, reactive-oxygen flag, conjugation station, except-acetylated chip, and excretion terminal) + blocks[2] the steps block distilling the same pipeline; the printed labels are also carried verbatim in blocks[1] the table block

textbookVisuals.sourceBook: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 2026
textbookVisuals.visualPurpose: The metabolism rules text block — the either/both + non-sequential intro rule, the geriatric rule, and the slow-acetylator rule (book 230, top half)
textbookVisuals.sourceFigureDescription: PURE TEXT (pdfimages: zero raster images; VLM confirmed): 'Drugs can be metabolized by either or both phase I and phase II reactions. These reactions serve to bioactivate or deactivate substances, and do not have to take place sequentially (eg, phase I can follow phase II, or take place as a single reaction). Geriatric patients lose phase I first. Patients who are slow acetylators have ↑ adverse effects from certain drugs because of ↓ rate of metabolism (eg, isoniazid).' No margin notes or mnemonics.
textbookVisuals.kypLocation: the registry visual's two clinical-rule cards (GERIATRIC RULE / SLOW-ACETYLATOR RULE) + the FORKS-NOT-A-LADDER banner and the phase I vs phase II comparison strip, with the rules also carried verbatim in the note's table block (rows INPUTS and PHASE I/II), core.what, and recall[0-2]

topics.title: Elimination of Drugs: Zero & First Order
topics.productionRationale: Zero-order (capacity-limited, constant amount: ethanol, aspirin, phenytoin at therapeutic doses) vs first-order (constant fraction) elimination, the PEA/amount-over-time figure and the steady-state/half-life rules. Shared page 252 with drug-metabolism, distinct subsections.

textbookVisuals.sourceBook: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 2026
textbookVisuals.visualPurpose: The two-column zero-order / first-order elimination text block (book 230)
textbookVisuals.sourceFigureDescription: PURE TEXT (pdfimages: zero raster images; VLM confirmed): the two-column elimination block — Zero-order elimination [Rate of elimination is constant regardless of Cp (ie, constant amount of drug eliminated per unit time); Cp ↓ linearly with time; Examples of drugs—Phenytoin, Ethanol, and Aspirin (at high or toxic concentrations → ↑ salicylate saturation → zero-order elimination); Capacity-limited elimination.; margin mnemonic “A PEA is round, shaped like the “0” in zeroorder.”] vs First-order elimination [Rate of first-order elimination is directly proportional to the drug concentration (ie, constant fraction of drug eliminated per unit time); Cp ↓ exponentially with time; Applies to most drugs.; Flow-dependent elimination.].
textbookVisuals.kypLocation: the registry visual's fork banner + mirror panel headers/markers (EliminationKineticsMap in visuals/pharm-p4.tsx) + blocks[1] the table block carried verbatim

textbookVisuals.sourceBook: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 2026
textbookVisuals.visualPurpose: The two vector elimination-curve figures (book 230): zero-order (constant 2 U/h, shrinking t1/2 brackets) and first-order (halving 4→2→1→0.5 U/h slopes, equal t1/2 brackets)
textbookVisuals.sourceFigureDescription: VECTOR LINE ART, no raster (pdfimages: zero raster images; labels read via the pdftotext text layer + VLM): FIGURE 1, Zero-order elimination — y-axis 'Drug plasma concentration ↑', x-axis 'Time (h)', a STRAIGHT declining line with constant slope chips '2 U/h' and an 'Elimination rate (=slope)' label, half-life brackets 'First t1/2 > Second t1/2 > Third t1/2' (VLM: the FIRST bracket, at the highest concentration, is drawn longest), annotation 'Time of t1/2 ↑ as concentration ↑'. FIGURE 2, First-order elimination — same axes, an EXPONENTIAL decay curve whose 'Elimination rate (=slope)' chips halve 4 U/h → 2 U/h → 1 U/h → 0.5 U/h, equal brackets 'First t1/2 = Second t1/2 = Third t1/2', annotation 'Time of t1/2 is constant as concentration ↑'.

topics.title: Urine pH, Ion Trapping & Dosage Calculations
topics.productionRationale: Weak acid/base ion trapping in urine (the aspirin overdose bicarbonate rule) + loading dose vs maintenance dose calculations with the Cp target equations.

textbookVisuals.sourceBook: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 2026
textbookVisuals.visualPurpose: The Urine pH and drug elimination text/equations block + the Dosage calculations block (book 231)
textbookVisuals.sourceFigureDescription: PURE TEXT + TYPESET EQUATIONS (pdfimages: zero raster images; VLM confirmed): the rule 'Ionized species are trapped in urine and cleared quickly. Neutral forms can be reabsorbed.'; the weak-acid block (RCOOH (lipid soluble) ↔ RCOO– + H+ (trapped); examples phenobarbital, methotrexate, aspirin (salicylates); treat overdose with sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize urine); the weak-base block (RNH3+ (trapped) ↔ RNH2 + H+ (lipid soluble); examples TCAs, amphetamines; trapped in acidic environments; for severe alkalosis treat with ammonium chloride to acidify urine); the pKa definition (pH at which drugs (weak acid or base) are 50% ionized and 50% nonionized; represents the strength of the weak acid or base); the TCA rule (sodium bicarbonate to overcome the sodium channel-blocking activity — treats cardiac toxicity, does not accelerate drug elimination); and the dosage block (Loading dose = Cp × Vd / F; Maintenance dose = Cp × CL × τ / F; Cp = target plasma concentration; τ = dosage interval, does not apply for continuous infusions; renal/liver disease → maintenance dose ↓, loading dose usually unchanged; time to steady state depends primarily on t1/2, independent of dose and dosing frequency).
textbookVisuals.kypLocation: the registry visual (Band 1 the tubular trapping map with the blood strip, the two equilibrium cards, and the NaHCO3/NH4Cl treatment arrows; Band 3 the TCA exception card with the renal-vs-cardiac contrast chips; Band 4 the dosage panel — UrinePhTrappingMap in visuals/pharm-p5.tsx) + blocks[1] and blocks[5] the table blocks carried verbatim + blocks[2] the compare block

textbookVisuals.sourceBook: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 2026
textbookVisuals.visualPurpose: The ionization-vs-pH curve — the vector figure on book 231
textbookVisuals.sourceFigureDescription: The ONE vector figure on the page (zero rasters; VLM confirmed the topology): a graph titled 'Ionized species formation (%)' with a y-axis 0-100 (ticks 0, 50, 100) against an x-axis 'pH' running 4-14 (ticks 4, 8, 12, 14); two S-shaped curves labeled 'Weak acid' (rising to the right — more ionized at high pH) and 'Weak base' (falling to the right — more ionized at low pH) crossing at the 50% level near pH 9-10, with dashed horizontal (50%) and vertical (crossing-pH) guide lines; the annotation 'pKa: 9.2' sits below the x-axis near the crossing, flanked by the margin notes 'pKa = more acidic' (toward low pH) and 'pKa = more basic' (toward high pH) with arrows. topics.title: Efficacy vs Potency: Reading Dose-Response Curves
topics.productionRationale: Efficacy (Emax, the ceiling) vs potency (EC50, the shift) on the dose-response curve — which the exam tests with partial agonists, competitive antagonists, and the EC50-shift questions.

topics.title: Receptor Binding, Agonist Types & Therapeutic Index
topics.productionRationale: The A/B/C receptor-binding panels (full/partial agonists, antagonists, inverse agonists) with the Can/Cannot behaviors + the therapeutic index TD50/ED50 with the margin-of-safety reading.

topics.title: Drug Effect Modifications
topics.productionRationale: Potentiation, additive/synergistic effects, tolerance, tachyphylaxis, and the placebo/nocebo framework. Shared page 256 with autonomic-receptors, distinct subsections.

topics.title: Autonomic Receptors: The Organ Response Table
topics.productionRationale: The organ-by-organ autonomic table (eye, heart, vasculature, GI, GU, sweat glands with the sympathetic-cholinergic exception) — THE master table of autonomic pharmacology. Shared page 256 with drug-effect-modifications.

topics.title: Acetylcholine Receptors: Nicotinic & Muscarinic
topics.productionRationale: Nm (somatic muscle), Nn (all autonomic ganglia, adrenal medulla), M1-M3 muscarinic — the binding/activation hierarchy (nerve gas: irreversible; curare: Nn reversible) with the agonist/antagonist matrix. Shared page 257 with pain-transmission.

topics.title: Pain Transmission & Analgesic Targets
topics.productionRationale: The pain fiber table (A-delta fast/sharp vs C slow/burning), the gate-control and descending modulation pathways, and where opioids/NSAIDs/TCAs act. Shared page 257 with acetylcholine-receptors.

topics.title: Micturition Control: The Bladder Pharmacology
topics.productionRationale: The detrusor/sphincter parasympathetic-sympathetic wiring with the Botox/anticholinergic/α-blocker intervention points for urge vs overflow incontinence. Shared page 258 with adrenergic-receptor-distribution.

topics.title: Tissue Distribution of Adrenergic Receptors
topics.productionRationale: α1/α2/β1/β2/β3 receptor distribution by tissue (the B1 one-heart/B2 two-lungs rule) with the vaso, bronchi, and uterine targets. Shared page 258 with micturition-control.

topics.title: G-Protein-Linked Second Messengers
topics.productionRationale: The complete Gs/Gi/Gq table — adrenergic (α1 q, α2 i, β1/β2/β3 s), muscarinic (M1 q, M2 i, M3 q), dopaminergic, and the rest with their second messengers (cAMP, IP3/DAG/Ca2+) and major functions. The single highest-yield table in autonomic pharmacology.

topics.title: Autonomic Drugs: Synapse Targets & Overview
topics.productionRationale: The NE-release modulation (α2 autoreceptor negative feedback), amphetamine/VMAT/NET mechanism, and the cholinergic vs noradrenergic synapse figure with every drug's entry point (ChAT, botulinum, AChE, MAO, COMT, reserpine, guanethidine).

topics.title: Cholinomimetic Agents
topics.productionRationale: Direct agonists (bethanechol, carbachol, methacholine, pilocarpine — with the source's own mnemonics) vs indirect anticholinesterases (edrophonium, pyridostigmine, echothiophate, the organophosphates + pralidoxime reactivation rule) with applications and the COPD/asthma/peptic-ulcer exacerbation warning.

topics.title: Muscarinic Antagonists & Atropine
topics.productionRationale: The anticholinergic system reference table (atropine, benztropine, scopolamine, ipratropium, oxybutynin, the SOFT/BENZ mnemonic families) + the atropine block with DUMBBELSS and the temperature-regulation rule.

topics.title: Sympathomimetics
topics.productionRationale: The α1/α2/β1/β2/D1 receptor map with direct (epi, NE, isoproterenol, phenylephrine, dopamine, dobutamine), indirect (amphetamines, ephedrine), and mixed (cocaine, TCAs, MAOIs) sympathomimetics — hemodynamics, indications, and the epinephrine-reversal experiment. topics.title: Sympatholytics (α2-agonists) & α-Blockers
topics.productionRationale: The α2-agonists (clonidine, guanfacine, α-methyldopa with the pregnancy/Coombs rules, tizanidine) + the α-blockers (phenoxybenzamine irreversible for pheochromocytoma, phentolamine, the selective α1 blockers with the first-dose hypotension rule).

topics.title: β-Blockers
topics.productionRationale: The full β-blocker table — the drug list with selectivity/ISA properties, and the nine applications (angina, glaucoma, heart failure with the mortality trio bisoprolol/carvedilol/metoprolol, hypertension, thyroid storm, HCM, migraine, MI) with actions and the contraindication traps.

topics.title: Phosphodiesterase Inhibitors
topics.productionRationale: The PDE inhibitor table — nonspecific (theophylline, methylxanthines with cardiotoxicity/neurotoxicity), PDE-5 (sildenafil with the NO/cGMP mechanism and the nitrates contraindication), PDE-3 (milrinone), PDE-4 (roflumilast) with mechanisms, uses, and adverse effects.

topics.title: Ingested Seafood & Plant Toxins
topics.productionRationale: The seafood toxin table (ciguatera, scombroid with the MAOI interaction, shellfish/saxitoxin, pufferfish/tetrodotoxin) + the plant toxins (anticholinergic plants, ricin, cyanogenic with the bitter-almond rule, convulsions water hemlock).

topics.title: Specific Toxicity Treatments: The Antidote Table
topics.productionRationale: THE antidote table — acetaminophen (N-acetylcysteine), organophosphates (atropine + pralidoxime), methanol/ethylene glycol (fomepizole/dialysis), iron (deferoxamine), copper/arsenic/gold (dimercaprol), lead (EDTA/succimer), methemoglobinemia (methylene blue), cyanide (nitrite + thiosulfate), opioids, benzos, TCAs, warfarin, heparin — the highest-yield table in toxicology.

topics.title: Drug Reactions: Endocrine & Reproductive
topics.productionRationale: The endocrine/reproductive adverse-reaction table — from gynecomastia (spironolactone, cimetidine) to SIADH/hyponatremia (carbamazepine, SSRIs), adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism/hyperthyroidism, and the sexual-dysfunction families.

topics.title: Drug Reactions: Hematologic
topics.productionRationale: The hematologic adverse-reaction table — aplastic anemia (chloramphenicol, carbamazepine), agranulocytosis (methimazole, clozapine), megaloblastic (methotrexate, phenytoin), hemolysis (G6PD drugs, penicillin, methyldopa), SLE-like, thrombocytopenia, and the gray-baby/serotonin-syndrome classics.

topics.title: Drug Reactions: Neurologic
topics.productionRationale: The neurologic adverse-reaction table — seizures (bupropion, INH, the withdrawn drugs), tremor/other movement disorders (tardive dyskinesia, Parkinsonism), headache, peripheral neuropathy (INH, vincristine, metronidazole), and the cognitive effects.

topics.title: Drugs Affecting Pupil Size & CYP-450 Interactions
topics.productionRationale: The mydriasis/miosis drug lists (the classic pin-point-opioids vs blown-out-atropine/amphetamine/CO pairing) + the CYP-450 table of selected inducers (the chronic alcohol/phenytoin/rifampin family) and inhibitors (the cimetidine/erythromycin/ketoconazole/GFJ family).

topics.title: Drug Names: Prefixes, Suffixes & Stem Families
topics.productionRationale: The drug-name tables across both pages — the -prazole PPIs, -sartan ARBs, -olol β-blockers, -afil PDE-5s, -statin/-vastatin, gli- antidiabetics, -caine anesthetics, -pril ACEs, the dofa-/gab- families, and the suffix-to-class decoding rules.

topics.title: Biologic Agents
topics.productionRationale: The biologic agents table — the -mab monoclonal antibody families (the -xi-/-zu- humanization codes), the -cept fusion proteins, recombinant cytokines and enzymes, with their targets and indications.
